title: What Holds This Paper Up
intro: The tour retells this paper front to back, section by section, in the order the authors wrote it. This read does something else: it follows the dependencies between the paper's parts, so that a choice made in section 2 can be put next to the number it produces in section 4, and a defect introduced in one place next to the repair offered somewhere else. What comes out is a set of chains, borrowed assumptions and admitted gaps that no single section states. Where the paper hedges, these chapters hedge with it, and where the evidence is thinner than the claim, they say so.
unusedNote:
One edge is not used anywhere: e080 (a dictionary learning run is one instance of the sparse autoencoder). It is pure notation — it explains that the middle number in "A/1/3450" names the run — and it carries no claim that a cross-cutting chapter could turn into an insight. The feature-notation scheme is used throughout the chapters without being argued about.

Everything else appears in exactly one chapter's edgeIds; no edge is double-counted, so the coverage list is also a partition. All 57 edges marked [load-bearing] are placed.

Two honest qualifications about depth rather than coverage. First, the four chapters marked for expansion carry 15–25 edges each, and their bodies name only some of those explicitly — the DNA and Hebrew proxy disagreements (e040, e041, e043, e067, e069), the tokenizer motifs (e015, e017, e052, e086, e088), the density diagnostics (e007, e058, e090) and the automated-scoring machinery (e046, e094, e099) are drawn on as a group and belong to the child pages, not the parent bodies. Second, the edge-themes were used as raw material only: [[etheme-why-dictionary-learning]] is split between chapters one and two, [[etheme-proxies-and-specificity]] between four and five, and [[etheme-population-scale-evidence]] between five and seven, because in each case the theme bundles a method choice together with the evidence that later strains it, and the strain is the point.

chapters.title: The method was picked twice by elimination, and the second time for being weak
chapters.body:
The sparse autoencoder is not put forward here as the best available way to decompose a layer. It is what survives two separate eliminations, and the second one selects deliberately against capability.

Take the first. [[superposition]] is the hypothesis that a layer represents more distinct features than it has neurons, by giving each feature its own direction in activation space instead of its own unit. An earlier paper by the same group set out three strategies for dealing with it. One was to build models that never form superposition at all, and the authors say they spent significant time on that route [[architectural-approaches-to-superposition]].

They report that it failed, and not in the way they expected. They had assumed the price would be a performance hit. What they found was that removing superposition does not buy interpretability in the first place.

They trained subject models with sparsity forced into their own activations, pushed as far as one-hot [[activation-sparsity-training]]. That does eliminate superposition. The neurons stayed polysemantic anyway — one unit still responding to a mixture of unrelated inputs, the condition [[polysemanticity]] names and the thing the whole programme is trying to escape.

The reason is a four-feature toy calculation, and it repays walking [[cross-entropy-favors-polysemanticity]]. One binary neuron; four mutually exclusive features A, B, C, D, each predicting its own next token. Let the neuron fire on A alone and predict A correctly, predicting uniformly over B, C and D otherwise. The cross-entropy loss is $\frac{3}{4}\ln 3 \approx 0.8$. Now let it fire on both A and B, predicting uniformly over those two, and uniformly over C and D when silent. The loss is $\ln 2 \approx 0.7$.

The ambiguous neuron wins.

Under mean squared error the two arrangements can tie, and for some feature importance curves the clean one is preferred [[mse-loss-and-monosemanticity]]. Language models are trained with cross-entropy. So the loss function, not the architecture, settles it. [[solu]], an earlier activation function meant to pull features into the neuron basis, gets the same verdict in miniature: some neurons cleaner, others worse, and no total accounting offered.

That leaves [[dictionary-learning]] — writing each activation as a sparse combination of directions drawn from an oversized set. Here the second elimination runs.

The hard inner problem is compressed sensing, which in exact form is NP-hard [[np-hardness-of-exact-sparse-recovery]]. The transformer is certainly not solving an NP-hard problem when it reads its own activations. So a sophisticated recovery method might dig out structure the model has no way to use, which is the stated reason for wanting a deliberately weak one [[weak-dictionary-learning]].

Classical algorithms such as Method of Optimal Directions and K-SVD were tried and set aside [[classical-dictionary-learning-algorithms]], partly on scale: the autoencoder trains on 8 billion activation vectors. And [[disentanglement]], which looks for at most as many factors as there are dimensions, is ruled out by the demand for more directions than dimensions.

chapters.title: Features are directions by construction, so the method cannot discover that they are not
chapters.body:
Four assumptions are fixed before any training data is touched. A successful fit is then evidence that those assumptions are workable — not evidence that they are true, and the method has no way to report that any of them is wrong.

The decomposition is stated first, on its own terms: each token's MLP activation vector is a fixed bias plus a weighted sum of unit vectors, one per feature [[linear-feature-decomposition]]. [[eq-feature-decomposition]] is where the unit vector gets its name. A [[feature-direction]] is what a feature writes along when it fires. The scalar weight riding on it is the [[feature-activation]], and in the trained autoencoder that number is a linear readout of the shifted activation plus a bias, passed through a ReLU [[eq-encoder]].

So "a feature is a direction" is not a finding. It is the shape of the factorization. It comes in from the [[linear-representation-hypothesis]], the claim that networks represent meaningful properties as directions in activation space. A property represented some other way has nowhere to go in this equation.

Second, width. The dictionary is deliberately made wider than the 512-dimensional vector it decomposes — [[overcompleteness]]. That is only sensible if you believe the layer packs more features than it has neurons, which is exactly what superposition asserts.

Overcompleteness then forces something. You cannot fit more than 512 mutually perpendicular directions into a 512-dimensional space. Once there are more directions than that, some pairs must have a nonzero dot product. Switching one feature on slightly switches its neighbours on, and the paper calls that cross-talk [[interference]].

Why is interference tolerable? That is the third assumption. [[noisy-simulation]] describes the small network as approximately simulating a larger, sparser one, and it works only if [[feature-sparsity]] holds — few features active on any given token, so non-orthogonal directions rarely fire together. If many fired at once, interference would be constant rather than occasional.

Fourth, the sparsity itself is borrowed rather than derived. The autoencoder is trained so most hidden units are exactly zero on any token, on the strength of [[sparsity-of-natural-latent-variables]], a long-standing hypothesis that the latent variables behind natural data are mostly inactive at any moment. Nothing about the transformer establishes it.

Only after all four does the [[sparse-autoencoder]] appear, and it appears as the concrete way to obtain a decomposition of that shape: the hidden units supply the weights, and the columns of the output matrix supply the directions. That is why [[dictionary-decoder]] and "dictionary" are used interchangeably throughout.

Put side by side, these are inputs. The method can certainly fail — it can find nothing interpretable. What it cannot do is tell you that a property is represented non-linearly, or that this layer is not in superposition after all.

chapters.title: One hyperparameter decides every reported number, and no measurement can check it
chapters.body:
There is a single dial that determines everything the paper reports about a run, and the paper states plainly that it has no metric able to say whether the dial was set correctly. That admission sits in a short subsection early on, and every headline figure later depends on it.

The method is one loss with exactly two terms [[eq-autoencoder-loss]]. Squared error between the MLP activation and its reconstruction, plus an L1 penalty on the hidden activations [[l1-sparsity-penalty]]. The first term wants a close match, which is easiest when many features are active. The second charges for every unit of activation, which drives most feature activations to exactly zero. The [[l1-coefficient]] is the exchange rate between them.

One guard is needed before that penalty means anything. The charge falls on the activations, so shrinking every activation lowers the loss — and the decoder could grow its columns to compensate, leaving the reconstruction unchanged and the penalty paid off for free. Fixing every dictionary column to L2 norm 1 closes that route [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]].

Now the problem. Training loss is the cheapest signal available, and it is used to compare optimizers and learning rates [[training-loss-metric]]. It cannot be compared across runs with different L1 coefficients, because changing the coefficient changes the loss function being measured. The hyperparameter most in need of choosing is the one the easy metric cannot speak to.

A better metric was attempted. An [[information-based-metric]] would score a factorization by the total information of autoencoder plus data. It did not track what the authors cared about: runs averaging hundreds of active features per token, but with low reconstruction error, could score better than sparser runs. It was abandoned.

What is left is a picture. [[l0-nll-tradeoff]] places every trained autoencoder by how few features fire per token against how much of the MLP layer's loss contribution it recovers [[fig-68]]. Run A/1 is sparse and recovers 79%; run A/5, with 131,072 features and a lower coefficient, recovers 94.5% while firing many more features per token. The coefficient is a point picked off that frontier by eye, and the stated preference is only a rough one — fewer than about ten or twenty active features per token.

The 79% needs its own unpacking [[loss-recovered-by-features]]. Splice the reconstruction in place of the real activations, and the model's loss rises by some amount. Divide that rise by the rise from deleting the MLP layer entirely [[zero-ablation-baseline]]. The ratio is 21%, so 79% is called recovered — and the paper adds that the ablated-MLP denominator may be an especially bad baseline, which would inflate the figure.

The measure they would rather have replaces activations with ones simulated from each feature's written explanation [[explanation-based-loss-measure]]. Their own estimate for the naive version is twelve to twenty-five thousand dollars to simulate 100k features over a single 4,096-token context. So the reconstruction number is reported instead.

That leaves [[feature-density]], the fraction of tokens on which a feature fires, as the working diagnostic — and it comes with its own caveat, since the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] visible in [[fig-64]] is read as a training artifact on anecdotal evidence.

chapters.title: The specificity case rests on a score the authors wrote, and where it disagrees they rule against it
chapters.body:
The central claim about any single feature is [[activation-specificity]]: if the feature is firing, the hypothesised context is present. It is ranked above [[activation-sensitivity]], the converse question of whether the feature is on whenever the context is there, on the grounds that polysemanticity shows up as a unit firing on clearly unrelated things.

Specificity needs a label for the text that does not come from the feature. Otherwise the argument is circular: the feature fires on Arabic because Arabic is where it fires.

So the paper builds a [[computational-proxy]] — a cheap per-token score for the hypothesised context, computed without reference to the feature. Every proxy has the same shape [[eq-proxy-loglikelihood-ratio]]: the log of how much likelier the string is under the guessed context than under text in general.

For a writing system, the numerator is the hard half. It would mean a generative model of Arabic text. Bayes' rule turns it into the probability of Arabic given the string, which is easy [[script-proxy-via-bayes]], and whether a character belongs to a script is not estimated at all — it is decided by [[unicode-block-detection]], for Arabic including U+0600–U+06FF and U+0750–U+077F.

The result is the paper's lead picture [[fig-8]]. Arabic script is 0.13% of training tokens and 81% of the tokens where [[arabic-script-feature]] is active. The support is uneven, and the paper says so: 98% above activation 5, but 25% where the feature barely fires. A single Pearson number folds both halves together at 0.74.

Sensitivity is where it gives way. The feature skips the definite-article prefix "ال" entirely, and that gap is covered by [[complementary-arabic-features]] rather than by this one. Nothing in the paper predicts which contexts get a family and which get a single feature — [[dna-feature]] appears to be alone in covering its own context. Both are context features, firing across a stretch of text rather than on one token.

The Arabic case is also the first full pass through [[feature-evidence-template]]: specificity, sensitivity, downstream effects, not-a-neuron, universality, in that order, reused by every later case study.

Now the part visible only with the cases side by side. The independence of the yardstick is what does the arguing — and the authors reserve the right to overrule it.

Base64 is where they exercise that right [[base64-proxy]]. Its correlation with the feature's activations is 0.38, against 0.74 for Arabic, the widest disagreement in the paper. The answer given is that the proxy is too broad rather than the feature impure: hexadecimal strings satisfy a model of base64 as random draws from [a-zA-Z0-9+/], and hexadecimal turns out to have a feature of its own [[hexadecimal-feature]].

That may well be right. Name the move anyway. The case where the independent measure disagrees most is settled by arguing against the measure, on a small hand-read sample, by the people whose feature is under test [[proxy-limitations]].

chapters.title: One linearity approximation carries both the logit weights and the excuse for the weak activations
chapters.body:
Two of the paper's arguments sit in different sections, look unrelated, and rest on the same claim. If that claim weakens, both weaken together.

Start with the summary quantity. A [[logit-weight]] is a single vector, one number per vocabulary token, saying how much a feature's firing moves that token's next-token logit. That is well defined only if the effect scales with the activation rather than changing shape as the activation grows [[linear-logit-effects]]. In a one-layer model the paper argues it is close to linear.

One correction is needed to get there. The path from an MLP direction to the logits runs through the final layer norm, which is not a linear map. It is approximated as a fixed mean-removing projection followed by a diagonal rescaling [[layer-norm-linearization]]. With that in place, the feature-to-logit path becomes a product of matrices.

[[fig-10]] shows the result for the Arabic feature: a fat mode at zero covering most of the vocabulary, plus a small mode far to the right holding Arabic characters and the byte tokens \xd8 and \xd9 that begin most Arabic UTF-8 encodings. The paper lists three ways this could overstate the feature's real influence [[logit-weight-caveats]].

Now the second argument, from a much later section. When each band of a feature's activation range is scored separately against the interpretation suggested by the whole spectrum [[activation-interval-analysis]], interpretability falls as activations get weaker [[fig-42]]. Some features hold across the top 60% and then drop away.

That would be tolerable if weak activations were rare. They are not. The paper states plainly that most actual activations are small, so most of them land in exactly the bands that score worst [[low-interval-activation-skew]].

The answer offered is [[large-activations-dominate]] — and it is the linearity claim again. If a feature's effect on the logits is linear in its activation, then twice the activation is twice the push, so getting the strong firings right matters more than getting the weak ones right. The same claim licenses the [[expected-value-plot]], which reweights the activation histogram by magnitude so a bar's height is total activation contributed rather than tokens counted [[fig-9]].

Read carefully, that redrawing does not clean up the impure low activations. It argues they matter less.

Two consequences follow. First, what answers the weak-activation problem is an argument, not a measurement of how much is left unexplained. Second, the paper is explicit that linearity here is a one-layer fact, and that in larger models the same claim rests on conjecture rather than a watertight argument.

A mechanism for the impurity is offered separately: if the dictionary holds fewer entries than the model has true features, the unrecovered ones would smear as weak activations across the learned ones [[autoencoder-width-limitation]]. That is plausible because [[feature-splitting]] keeps dividing features as the dictionary widens rather than exhausting them.

chapters.title: Two deflationary readings are argued away, and a third — the tokenizer — is accepted
chapters.body:
There are three ways to say a learned feature is not really about the model. The paper meets two and concedes the third, and the three defences are of very different strengths.

### It is only the data

Activations reflect both the dataset's distribution and what the model does to it, so features might be dataset correlations projected into a new space [[model-vs-data-question]]. The answer is structural rather than experimental. The autoencoder is fit to MLP activation vectors alone [[activations-only-decomposition]]; nothing about logits or next-token predictions enters its loss.

So a feature's downstream effect was never fitted. If it lines up with the feature's interpretation anyway, that agreement has to be a property of the model. The argument is strong precisely because it is about the objective, not about an experiment that could have gone either way.

The evidence it licenses comes in three forms. [[feature-ablation]] subtracts one feature's own contribution — its activation times its dictionary direction, leaving every other feature's contribution in place — and finishes the forward pass, so the change in per-token loss is measured rather than approximated [[fig-11]]. [[pinned-feature-sampling]] holds one feature at its maximum and samples: from the prefix 1,2,3,…,10 the continuation comes out in Arabic script [[fig-43]]. That last one is a single hand-chosen prompt on a single feature. It demonstrates rather than measures.

### It is only a neuron renamed

[[feature-neuron-nonalignment]] answers this by drawing the feature's decoder column one MLP neuron at a time [[fig-13]]. The three largest coefficients are negative, and 27 of the 512 neurons carry coefficients of at least 0.1 in magnitude. An outside researcher, invited before publication, trained his own autoencoder on a different one-layer model and found 4% of directions well explained by a single neuron, 4% by two to ten, and the remaining 92% dense [[external-replication]].

Note what that rules out and what it leaves. It rules out the feature being one neuron. It leaves open a small set of neurons cancelling into one. And the account of why the closest neuron mixes many languages [[mutually-exclusive-features-in-superposition]] is an interpretation of the picture, not something the picture tests.

### It is the tokenizer

This one the paper accepts [[tokenization-artifacts-in-features]]. [[byte-pair-encoding]] merges frequent byte sequences, so a token need not line up with a character, and non-Latin scripts arrive as several byte tokens — U+062B comes in as \xd8 then \xab.

That fact alone creates a motif: pairs of features handing off, one firing on the prefix byte and one on the suffix that completes the character [[unicode-token-state-machines]]. Nothing like it would exist if a character were one token. The same reading explains a feature that fires on lone digits inside base64 and then pushes the ten digit tokens down — two adjacent digits would have merged into one token, so a lone digit token is evidence the next character is not a digit.

Read through [[action-features]], where every feature both responds to something and raises the probability of something, these handoffs assemble into state machines, including a four-node one that produces valid HTML. The evidence for them is read off visualisations and logit weights, not tested by intervention.

chapters.title: The population evaluation was rebuilt to stop flattering itself, then both of its own controls went the wrong way
chapters.body:
The population-level evaluation is designed around a flaw the authors identify in standard practice, including their own earlier work. Then two controls they run on that evaluation come out against the result, and each is answered after the fact.

### The redesign

The usual way to interpret a unit is to read its [[top-dataset-examples]] and say what they have in common. Even a mixed unit looks coherent at its maximum, so top examples flatter polysemantic units. The fix is the [[activation-interval]]: cut each unit's range into eleven evenly spaced bands between zero and its maximum, and sample examples from every band.

[[manual-interpretability-scoring]] is built on that — 412 scored intervals across 162 features and neurons, on a 0–14 rubric, with the annotator under [[blinded-annotation]] as to whether he was looking at a feature or a neuron. The two distributions barely overlap [[fig-39]]: the median feature interval scores 12, the median neuron 0, meaning no hypothesis could be formed at all. The evidence is thinner than the gap sounds. One annotator, and he is one of the authors.

[[automated-interpretability]] buys scale instead of trust. A language model writes an explanation of a unit from examples where it fires; a second pass predicts that unit's activations on unseen text from the explanation alone, and the score is the rank correlation between prediction and truth over 60 nine-token examples. It measures anything only if nothing about the activations reaches the prediction step except the written words, which the paper treats as a design constraint [[no-activation-leakage]]. A companion test asks which unseen tokens the unit promotes: features 74%, neurons 58%, chance 50% [[automated-logit-scoring]]. A margin, not a separation.

One more thing belongs here. The four features studied in depth were chosen because simple proxies exist for them [[cherry-picked-case-studies]] — a proxy for "text concerning fantasy games" would be hard to build. So the deep evidence and the representative evidence are never available for the same features.

### The two controls

The first shuffles the entries inside each of the transformer's weight matrices and runs dictionary learning on that [[randomized-transformer]], so any structure recovered must come from the data rather than from what the model learned. On the automated activation score, the randomized model's features get a slightly higher median than the real ones [[fig-70]].

The response is to split the randomized features into [[single-token-features]] and the rest, and report that the real features win on the second cluster. The split is made after seeing the result, and the disagreement on the headline metric stands as stated.

The second control is [[importance-scoring]], the principled correction for the fact that scored examples were not sampled at random. Applying it collapses feature scores toward zero while barely moving neurons: 0.28 against 0.04.

The explanation given is about density, not quality [[importance-scoring-degeneracy]]. Feature densities run from about 1e-3 down to 1e-6, so nearly all the weight lands on random text where the feature never fires, and 88% of a feature's true activations there are zero against 54% for neurons. An explanation predicting zero everywhere then scores well.

chapters.title: The finding the authors least expected may have been produced by their own sparsity penalty
chapters.body:
The paper reports hundreds of separate features for the word "the" — "the" in physics distinct from "the" in mathematics — and says outright these are not what it expected to find. Placed next to the training objective, the finding has an uncomfortable reading, and the paper gives that reading first.

These are [[token-in-context-features]]: firing on one specific token, but only in one kind of surrounding text. In the vocabulary of representation schemes that is a [[local-code]] — one dedicated unit per thing represented, including per combination of properties [[local-vs-compositional-codes]]. The more intuitive alternative is a [[compositional-code]], with a unit for "the" and a separate unit for physics, active together.

Here is the problem. A local code is sparser than a compositional one, because one active unit covers the whole combination instead of two. The autoencoder is trained with a penalty that rewards exactly that.

So the first hypothesis for the paper's own token-in-context features is that its objective pushed too far toward sparsity, and that a better dictionary learning scheme might recover a more compositional set from the same transformer [[are-token-in-context-features-real]].

The counterargument is [[sharper-predictions-argument]], and it is about what each scheme can produce at the output. Under a compositional code the logits after "the" in physics are forced to be a sum: upweight tokens that follow "the", plus upweight tokens common in physics. A model wanting a sharper prediction than that sum has no way to get one. A dedicated feature can push exactly the tokens that follow "the" in physics writing.

That is a reason, and it is offered as one. It is not a measurement, and it is available at all only because a feature's effect on the logits can be read off directly.

The neighbouring observation makes the accounting harder rather than easier. Widening the autoencoder does not send features off to new parts of activation space; it divides the ones already there [[fig-46]]. A single feature that fires across whole base64 strings in the 512-unit dictionary becomes three in the 4,096-unit one — one preferring letters, one digits, one firing on base64 that decodes to readable ASCII [[fig-48]]. Links run both ways, so a feature at one width can both split and merge into the next.

The reading offered is [[dictionary-resolution]]: dictionary size is a zoom level on a conjectured set of [[true-features]] clustered tightly in superposition, not a guess at a correct count.

That clustering forces a revision elsewhere. The picture inherited from the earlier toy work had features spread roughly evenly, pushed apart by interference. Projected together, conceptually related directions instead sit at small angles and form tight clusters [[feature-geometry-clusters]], visible as families in [[fig-44]].

[[theories-of-superposition]] is rewritten to fit, and the paper says it does not know which account is right: features clumping while staying one-dimensional, or [[feature-manifolds]], continuous families of related directions — under which asking for the correct number of features may not be a well-posed question at all.

chapters.title: Universality holds for when features fire and largely fails for what they do
chapters.body:
The universality result is usually quoted as one number. There are two measures behind it, they disagree, and the paper reports the disagreement rather than burying it.

[[feature-universality]] asks whether a feature is a fact about the model rather than about one training run. Answering that needs a second model. [[transformer-a-and-b]] is the same architecture, the same data and the same hyperparameters, differing only in random seed, with its own separate dictionary learning run — a second instance of the same [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] rather than a different experiment.

Matching is done by [[activation-similarity]]: for each feature in A, take the feature in B whose activations have the highest [[pearson-correlation]] over 40 million dataset examples. The Arabic feature comes back as B/1/1334 [[fig-19]]. Across the whole population the median match is 0.72 for features and 0.46 for the two models' neurons [[feature-vs-neuron-universality]], shown as two histograms in [[fig-52]]. That population comparison is the strongest version of the claim in the paper.

Now the second measure. [[logit-weight-similarity]] compares matched features by what they do rather than when they fire, correlating their logit weight vectors over the vocabulary. For the Arabic pair, activation correlation is 0.91 and logit weight correlation is 0.23.

Across thousands of matched pairs the pattern holds: agreement on firing is consistently higher than agreement on downstream effect. The sharpest case is A/1/3949 and B/1/3321, correlated 0.98 on activations and negatively on logit weights, yet both firing on PLoS journal abbreviations and both predicting the period that follows [[fig-53]].

Two features can be doing the same job and score as opposites. That is what makes this a problem about the measure, and it is treated as one.

The account offered is [[weight-interference]]. A feature's logit weight histogram has a tall mode near zero and a small mode far to the right; the right mode is the deliberate effect, holding tokens specific to the feature's context, while the central mode is crosstalk forced by superposition rather than anything the model wants. Correlating full weight vectors therefore correlates mostly noise. That is a hypothesis, and it is not tested here.

The repair is [[attribution-similarity]]. For each sampled datapoint, take the feature's activation there and multiply it by its logit weight on the token that actually came next [[eq-attribution-vector]]. Stack those into a vector and correlate across models. The near-zero entries stop dominating, and the correlations track activation similarity closely — which is the paper's justification for using activation correlation throughout.

The shape of that repair matters. The measure that restores the agreement is itself built out of logit weights, weighted by the activations that already agreed. It is not an independent check on the disagreement it resolves.

The stronger test is left mostly open: whether these features match units other researchers found in other models [[universality-with-the-literature]]. A base64 neuron reported earlier in a SoLU model is offered as one such match, alongside hexadecimal and all-caps neurons.

i-the-dial-and-the-missing-metric.title: The histogram that stands in for the missing metric
i-the-dial-and-the-missing-metric.intro: The parent left feature density as the working diagnostic, with a caveat attached to it. This level opens the histogram itself: what the two humps are, how a count of dead units misses the population that matters, and the two extra per-feature numbers the paper reaches for when the humps merge in its widest runs.

chapters.title: What the histogram counts
chapters.body:
A feature's density is one number. It is the fraction of tokens in the training set on which that feature's activation is nonzero [[feature-density]].

Because the encoder ends in a ReLU, most activations on any given token are exactly zero. So density counts how often a unit fires at all, not how hard it fires when it does.

The numbers involved are very small, so the [[feature-density-histogram]] is drawn against $\log_{10}$ of density rather than density itself. A feature plotted at $-7$ fires on about one token in ten million. One plotted at $-4$ fires on one in ten thousand.

The paper has a hypothesis about why there should be a distribution here at all. It supposes the language model contains many features spread across a range of densities, and that rarer features are harder for the autoencoder to find simply because they turn up less often in training. That is the stated reason for harvesting activations over 40 million contexts [[autoencoder-training-dataset]].

Two quantities get read off the shape. How many features were recovered, and how rare the rarest recovered feature is. The appendix adds a third [[feature-density-diagnostics]]: the number of features with density above 1%, which the paper reads as a sign that the [[l1-coefficient]] has been set too low.

That third number is the interesting one. It is a statement about the coefficient, produced by a diagnostic that the coefficient does not invalidate.

A density is a property of the finished dictionary, not a value of the objective that trained it, so two runs fitted under different coefficients can be laid on the same axis and compared. The paper never says this in so many words — it simply uses the histogram that way — so read the reason as my reading rather than its argument.

The paper is careful about the standing of all this. It calls these metrics a decent proxy for subjective autoencoder performance, says so anecdotally, and adds that it has identified only some desiderata for the density distribution, with much still not understood. That admission is what stops the histogram from being a clear signal of progress.

chapters.title: Two modes, opposite interpretability
chapters.body:
The worked example is run A/16, one of the trained autoencoders [[dictionary-learning-run]]. Its histogram has two humps, and the paper says bimodality of this kind is typical rather than peculiar to that run.

The left hump sits around $10^{-7}$. The tallest bar there holds roughly 7,500 features, all firing on about one token in ten million. The right hump peaks near $10^{-5}$ and thins out past $10^{-3}$.

The paper names the right mode the [[high-density-cluster]] and says immediately that the name is relative. A feature at $10^{-5}$ is silent on 99.999% of tokens. Nothing in this picture is dense in any ordinary sense.

Then the claim that gives the histogram its use. Almost all of the features in the right mode are interpretable, and almost none of the features in the left mode are.

That is reported anecdotally. No score is attached, no sample is described, and no rubric is applied — even though the paper elsewhere builds a 0–14 rubric for exactly this kind of judgement. The diagnostic that stands in for the missing metric rests, at its centre, on an unscored impression.

Two hedges travel with the figure. The right mode may itself be split into two modes, one near $10^{-5}$ and another near $10^{-3}$, and the authors say they are still investigating what that split is.

The second hedge is offered as a suspicion about someone else's result. An outside report had found a bimodal distribution of cross-dictionary matches — take each feature in one trained dictionary, find its closest counterpart in a second dictionary by cosine similarity, and collect those similarities [[mean-max-cosine-similarity]]. The paper suggests its own density bimodality might partly explain that, since a population of ultralow features would not be expected to match across dictionaries and would form a second mode.

It is raised as an aside, with no test behind it.

chapters.title: Dead, and dead in practice
chapters.body:
The paper states the outcome it would like. Every autoencoder neuron should be either a meaningful feature or completely dead.

Training does deliver some of the second kind. A unit whose pre-ReLU input is negative on essentially every datapoint outputs nothing and receives no gradient, so it stays where it is [[dead-neurons]].

Many units land in neither category. The paper tentatively names the third group the ultralow density cluster.

The counts come from run A/1, the 4,096-feature dictionary the paper analyses in detail. Of those 4,096, 168 are dead — active on none of the 100 million dataset examples checked. A further 292 are ultralow: active on fewer than one example in a million, and exhibiting what the paper calls other atypical properties. Both groups are excluded from every later analysis.

So 460 units, a little over 11% of the dictionary, are set aside. A zero-activity check finds 168 of them and misses 292 [[de-facto-dead-neurons]].

The paper's argument for why that gap is real, rather than a threshold artifact, comes from the training curve. Train for more steps and the network kills off more of these ultralow neurons. A unit that longer training would have extinguished is, at the step count actually used, dead in practice while still counting as alive.

That is the stated reason for tracking the size of the high-density cluster instead of the dead-neuron count.

The same quantity is also what the paper's fix is tuned against. Dead units are periodically reinitialized toward inputs the autoencoder currently reconstructs worst [[neuron-resampling]], and the reported benefit of doing so is an increase in the number of high-density-cluster features.

The paper reads the ultralow cluster as an artifact of autoencoder training and not a real property of the transformer, and says it is still investigating the cause.

Its own comments section prints a replication that pushes the other way. Training on a different open-source one-layer model, the replicator found no dead features but more than half of all features below $10^{-4}$, almost all of them sharing a single encoder direction — one input fired 95% of them. The same direction formed across random seeds, which he reads as a fact about the model rather than an autoencoder artifact. Training an autoencoder orthogonal to that direction produced a fresh ultra-low cluster in a new direction.

The paper publishes this and does not reconcile it with its own reading.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: When density alone stops separating
chapters.body:
The clean gap is not guaranteed. The paper reports that in small preliminary experiments the two clusters are often perfectly separable, and that for runs with many autoencoder neurons and a large L1 coefficient they often overlap.

Run A/5 is the illustration. Its dictionary has 131,072 hidden units fitted to a 512-neuron MLP layer, 256 times as many directions as dimensions [[expansion-factor]].

Its histogram has no valley. Left of about $10^{-6.2}$ there are a few short isolated bars. From there the counts climb without a break to a single tall mass peaking near $10^{-5.7}$ at roughly 9,650 features, then fall away in a tail that fades out near $10^{-2.6}$.

There is nothing in that shape marking where the ultralow features stop. Note also what the axis cannot hold: a unit that never fires has density exactly zero, which has no position on a log scale, so the strictly dead units are absent from the picture by construction.

The fallback is to add two more numbers per feature [[density-cluster-separation]].

The first is that feature's entry of the encoder bias, the vector added before the ReLU [[autoencoder-encoder]]. Every plotted value is negative, running from about $-3$ down to about $-22$. Read it as a firing threshold: the input's projection onto the feature's read-in direction has to clear that magnitude before anything gets through.

The second is the dot product between the feature's decoder column and its encoder row. The decoder column is the direction the feature writes along, held at unit norm; the encoder row is the direction it reads with.

That second number carries information only because the two were learned separately. The encoder is not constrained to be the decoder's transpose [[untied-decoder-weights]], and the replicator measured a median cosine similarity of only about 0.5 between them across features. Had the weights been tied, the quantity would have been near-constant and useless as a discriminator.

Plotted along all three, the high-density cluster comes out as a compact island. Density alone does not cut it, bias alone does not cut it, and the dot product alone does not cut it — the high-density blob sits near $+1$ while the ultralow mass spreads across most of the $-3$ to $+3$ range.

Separability is what the figure shows, and separability is all it shows. It supplies a rule for drawing the boundary. It is not evidence that the units on the far side are a training artifact; that reading still rests on the two observations from the previous chapter.

chapters.title: What the histogram claims, and what it leaves out
chapters.body:
The diagnostic is also used to make a substantive claim, not just to grade runs.

The appendix lays out five panels, one per setting of the sparsity weight — 0.001, 0.004, 0.006, 0.008 and 0.01. Each panel overlays six density histograms, for dictionaries of 512, 4,096, 16,384, 32,768, 65,536 and 131,072 units, all fitted to the same 512-neuron layer.

Read one panel in order of width and two things happen at once.

The curves get taller. That is expected and carries nothing: the y axis is a raw count, not normalized by dictionary size, so more units mechanically means more counts.

The left edge keeps sliding further left. The rarest feature recovered keeps getting rarer at every size tried.

That second movement is the argument. Had the 512-neuron layer's features been exhausted, extra dictionary capacity should have gone dead or produced duplicates. Instead new mass keeps appearing in the rare tail.

The caption says this suggests the features have not been exhausted, and the hedge is earned. The plot counts features and cannot tell a genuinely new one from [[feature-splitting]] of a feature already present.

There is a second limit the paper supplies but does not apply here. The tall left-edge spikes in the $\lambda=0.008$ and $\lambda=0.01$ panels are precisely the large-width, large-coefficient regime where the paper says the two clusters overlap, so those spikes cannot be read as all real features. Applying that caveat to this figure is my reading, not the paper's.

The panels also show what raising the coefficient does. At $\lambda=0.001$ a bump sits to the right of $10^{-2}$ — features firing on more than 1% of tokens, which the paper's own checklist reads as the penalty being too weak. By $\lambda=0.01$ nothing survives above $10^{-2}$.

One thing the histogram never speaks to. It counts how often features fire, and says nothing about whether the reconstruction preserves what the model does.

That is the other reading entirely: average features active per token against fraction of the MLP layer's loss contribution recovered. The paper reports both and never states a relation between them, so a run that gains high-density features has not thereby been shown to move on the frontier.

i-a-yardstick-the-authors-built.title: Four correlation numbers, four different yardsticks
i-a-yardstick-the-authors-built.intro: The parent named one disagreement, base64 at 0.38. Here is the whole catalogue at working resolution: how each proxy is actually assembled, which cell of which grid each failure sits in, and why the four reported correlations — 0.8, 0.74, 0.55, 0.38 — are not measurements of the same thing.

chapters.title: The DNA proxy is reshaped three times before it is scored
chapters.body:
The [[dna-proxy]] uses the character-set recipe rather than the Bayes one [[character-distribution-proxy]]. DNA is modelled as a string drawn uniformly from four letters, so each character gets probability $1/4$. The denominator — text in general — is a product of independent per-token unigram probabilities [[unigram-p-s-estimate]].

Walk a short case. Six characters of ATCG have probability $4^{-6} \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-4}$ under the DNA model. Under the unigram model of ordinary text, a run of six uppercase letters confined to those four is much rarer than that, so the ratio is large and its log is comfortably positive.

Now three reshapings, each of which the paper states.

First, the proxy is never evaluated on one token. CAT is a single vocabulary token, and it occurs in nucleotide sequences and in English. A one-token score cannot separate them, so the proxy only ever looks at groups of at least two tokens. That narrows what the yardstick is allowed to see.

Second, the score at a token is the maximum over prefixes ending at that token [[prefix-maximization]]. The stated reason is that a feature's activation can depend on preceding text — a script feature may build up over a long run. So the reported number is the best any ending-here window achieves, not the score of a fixed window.

Third, the log-probabilities come out strongly bimodal: a string is either clearly ATCG-like or clearly not. The paper reduces the continuous score to a yes/no value on its sign [[proxy-binarization]]. It is that binarized version which correlates 0.8 with the [[dna-feature]]'s activations in [[fig-20]].

So 0.8 is a correlation between a continuous activation and a binary label, with the cut placed after looking at the distribution. The Arabic 0.74 is also computed against a proxy thresholded at 0, so the two are more alike than the raw description suggests. Neither is a correlation between two continuous quantities.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

chapters.title: The grid, and the two cells that go the other way
chapters.body:
[[fig-21]] is the audit. It crosses four activation levels of the DNA feature — including the feature off entirely — against whether the proxy fires, and fills each cell with random examples. The point of the grid is to read disagreements one at a time instead of through a summary number [[proxy-limitations]].

The verdict: in all but two of the disagreements, the paper judges that the feature does indicate DNA and the proxy is the one at fault.

Two mechanisms are named. The space inside the triplets TGG AGT is not in the four-letter alphabet, so the string stops looking like a uniform ATCG draw and the ratio collapses. The paper spells this floor out only for base64, where a non-alphabet character is given probability $10^{-10}$; for DNA it states the alphabet and not the else-branch, so applying the same floor is a reading rather than a quotation.

The second is sharper. The feature fires on the "'-" in 5'-TCT, which is punctuation and not DNA, and the paper calls that firing productive because what follows should be DNA. It does not leave that as an interpretation of examples. Ablating the feature lowers the model's probability on the strings that follow, which is a causal check that does not use the proxy at all.

The third direction is the one where the proxy fires and the feature is silent. The paper says that example is a DNA sequence, and that the feature starts firing on the very next token. It generalises: the feature may miss the first few tokens of a sequence, but by the end of a long one it is the only feature active [[context-features]].

That last remark is worth holding onto. It describes an onset lag, not a coverage gap, and it is what separates DNA from the script cases [[arabic-script-feature]].

One honest gap. The text says "all but two" and never itemises which two. The disagreements it does discuss are all defended. A reader cannot reconstruct the two exceptions from what is written.

sections.title: The feature is not a neuron
The Feature Is Not A Neuron

chapters.title: Hebrew at 0.55, where the rule scores the spaces against the feature
chapters.body:
The [[hebrew-script-proxy]] is the Arabic construction with different codepoint ranges substituted in [[script-proxy-via-bayes]]. Bayes' rule supplies the hard term, and the easy term is decided by lookup [[unicode-block-detection]].

The lookup is all-or-nothing. If a string consists entirely of in-block characters, $P(\text{script} \mid s) = 1$. If it contains any character outside those blocks, $P(\text{script} \mid s)$ is set to $10^{-10}$. There is no proportion in between.

Spaces and punctuation are shared across writing systems and live in other Unicode blocks. So one space drops a window of Hebrew prose to the floor. Prefix maximization takes some of this back, since a shorter space-free window ending at the same token may still score high. But a token that is itself whitespace can never score as Hebrew under this rule.

The paper reads [[fig-33]] and says exactly this. Some of the non-Hebrew colour sitting in the strong activations is common characters from other blocks. The [[hebrew-feature]] is firing hard on tokens the proxy was built to call non-Hebrew.

A second piece of the 0.55 is coverage rather than error. Most Hebrew codepoints begin with the byte \xd7 in UTF-8, and the tokenizer hands that byte over as its own token [[utf8-multi-token-characters]]. A/1/416 does not take those; a companion feature, A/1/1016, fires on \xd7 and predicts the bytes that finish the character. That is the same split seen in Arabic, where the definite-article prefix goes to a sibling [[complementary-arabic-features]].

One item in the spectrum does go against the feature. It weakly activates on other languages written in non-Latin scripts, and the proxy is right to mark those. The paper reports the leak and offers no account of it beyond noting it is weak — which lands it in the region the paper has already argued matters least.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

chapters.title: What the catalogue does to the numbers
chapters.body:
Four correlations are reported, all as Pearson between a feature's activations and its own proxy [[feature-proxy-correlation]] [[pearson-correlation]]. DNA 0.8, Arabic 0.74, Hebrew 0.55, base64 0.38.

They are not four readings from one instrument. Two proxies come from Bayes plus a Unicode lookup; two from a uniform character model. One of the four is binarized. The Arabic figure is stated over 40 million tokens; the other three sections give no token count. A ranking across them is comparing constructions as much as features.

Coverage differs too. DNA appears to have one feature to itself, while Arabic, Hebrew and base64 each share their context with siblings. A feature that hands part of its territory to a companion will lose sensitivity without becoming any less pure — which is the paper's own reason for ranking [[activation-specificity]] above [[activation-sensitivity]].

Now put the failures side by side. A space inside TGG AGT: proxy at fault. The "'-" before DNA: feature defended, by ablation. A newline inside Arabic text: proxy at fault. Whitespace and punctuation in Hebrew: proxy at fault. Hexadecimal setting off the base64 score: proxy at fault, with [[hexadecimal-feature]] named as the real owner.

The catalogue runs one way. Not one entry concludes that the proxy caught something real about the feature. The only reported exception, the cell where the proxy fires alone, is also explained away as a lag.

Each ruling may well be correct. The effect on the numbers is what to watch. If the audits hold, every correlation is a floor and true agreement is higher than printed. But a floor the authors set by ruling on their own disagreements is not the same object as a measurement — and the paper uses the numbers in both roles, as evidence where they are high and as understatements where they are low.

The check that would separate the two is not run: no blind scoring, no proxy built by someone with nothing at stake. What is run is the ablations, which need no proxy. That is where the strongest item in this whole catalogue comes from.

i-what-the-features-are-not.title: The tokenizer showing through the features
i-what-the-features-are-not.intro: The parent named the tokenizer concession and moved on. This level walks the mechanism: what byte-pair encoding actually hands a one-layer model, how the prefix–suffix pair entered the paper as a leftover from a failed sensitivity number, why the base64 digit feature is an inference about the encoding rather than about content, and where the four-node HTML automaton's evidence stops.

chapters.title: A character does not arrive whole
chapters.body:
[[byte-pair-encoding]] starts from raw bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a single new token. Whatever survives that process is a token. For English, merging runs far enough that common words come through as one piece.

For a script that is rare in the corpus, merging stops earlier. The character arrives in pieces instead [[utf8-multi-token-characters]].

The pieces are UTF-8 bytes, and UTF-8 is coarse-to-fine. The Arabic character ث, codepoint U+062B, is tokenized as \xd8 followed by \xab. Hebrew works the same way: \xd7 is the first token of most characters in the basic Hebrew block. Tamil takes three bytes but still splits in two — ண, U+0BA3, comes in as \xe0\xae then \xa3.

The paper points out the structure inside that split. The first part roughly specifies which Unicode block the character is in. The second specifies which character within the block.

So the model faces two different prediction problems one position apart. Standing on a prefix byte, the next token is almost forced: some small set of suffix bytes completes the character. Standing on a suffix byte, the character is done, and what may follow is a new complete character or a new prefix.

This is already visible in the paper's flagship case study, before any motif is named. The Arabic script feature A/1/3450 typically fires only on the last token of a split character. That is a suffix-position feature, though the paper does not call it one there.

Note how that claim is stated. The word is "typically", and no fraction is given. The activation histograms are broken down by an Arabic-script score, not by position within a character, so the paper never measures how strictly the feature keeps to suffixes.

chapters.title: The second half of the pair arrives as an excuse
chapters.body:
The prefix–suffix pair does not enter the paper as a motif. It enters as an explanation for a number that came out low.

The [[hebrew-feature]] A/1/416 is scored against a hand-built [[hebrew-script-proxy]] — a per-token estimate of whether the text is Hebrew, decided by Unicode block rather than by any model. The Pearson correlation between proxy and feature is 0.55. The comparable Arabic number is 0.74.

The shortfall is on the sensitivity side: the feature is not on everywhere Hebrew is present. The paper attributes some of that to [[hebrew-continuation-feature]] A/1/1016, which fires on the \xd7 byte and predicts the bytes that finish the Hebrew codepoint. Coverage is shared between two features, so neither one tracks the proxy alone.

Only later is the arrangement named in general [[unicode-token-state-machines]]. And the generalisation is not uniform across scripts.

Tamil is the clean case. The character always splits, so two features suffice, one per position.

Chinese is not clean. Many common Chinese characters have their own dedicated tokens, so they never split at all. Chinese characters are also spread across many Unicode blocks, and those blocks are large and cut across the boundaries a byte prefix would draw.

The paper's reading of what the model does there is a genuine simplification. A complete character, it says, is in the same position as a suffix: both can be followed by either a new complete character or a new prefix. So the two observed features are not "first half" and "second half". One fires on complete characters and on suffixes; the other fires only on prefixes and predicts suffixes.

The state variable is not where you are inside a character. It is whether a prefix can come next.

That reduction is read off feature visualisations and logit weight plots [[fig-57]]. Nothing counts how many Chinese characters the pair actually covers.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

chapters.title: A feature that reads the encoding, not the text
chapters.body:
The [[base64-digit-feature]] was not sought. It fell out of an apparent bug in [[feature-splitting]] — the observation that widening the autoencoder divides one feature into several finer ones covering the same territory.

In the 512-feature dictionary A/0 there is one base64 feature, A/0/45, firing across whole base64 strings. In the 4,096-feature dictionary A/1 there are three, jointly covering it [[fig-48]]. A/1/2357 prefers letters, A/1/2364 prefers digits, and A/1/1544 fires on base64 that decodes to readable ASCII [[base64-feature-family]].

The finding is in the comparison of two of them. A/1/2357 and A/1/2364 push almost exactly the same tokens up. The one difference is that the digit feature gives the ten digit tokens much lower weight [[fig-49]].

A content-based reading has nothing to offer here. Base64 is modelled as a random draw over [a-zA-Z0-9+/], so a digit is no less likely after a digit than after a letter.

The tokenizer reading does the work [[tokenization-artifacts-in-features]]. Two adjacent digits are a frequent byte pair, so byte-pair encoding merged them into one token. The string [Bq][8][9][mp] therefore never appears in the training data; it is tokenized as [Bq][89][mp].

So a lone digit token is itself evidence about the next character. If another digit had followed, this token would not have been a lone digit. The feature suppresses digits because the tokenizer already told it they are gone.

That lowers loss on real data, which is why the model has reason to hold it.

The evidence is two [[logit-weight]] histograms and nothing else. No ablation is run on A/1/2364. The paper's own wording is that this is "likely an artifact of tokenization".

One link in the chain is asserted rather than checked, and this is my reading rather than the paper's. The argument needs every two-digit pair to be in the merge table. Byte-pair encoding merges frequent pairs, and the paper does not inspect the vocabulary to confirm that all hundred of them merged.

chapters.title: The loop closes outside the model
chapters.body:
Every feature in this model can be read twice [[action-features]]. It responds to something, and it raises the probability of something.

The second reading is on firmer ground here than it would be in a deep model. The only MLP is the last one, so its output goes into the residual stream and then straight to the unembedding. Layer norm is approximated as a fixed projection plus a diagonal rescaling, which leaves the path linear [[linear-logit-effects]]. A feature's effect on the logits is then close to a fixed vector times its activation, and "what this feature does" becomes something you can plot.

Chain that reading across positions and you get the paper's automata [[finite-state-automata-features]]. The paper is explicit that these are not circuits. The features are not wired to each other inside the network.

What happens instead is this. A feature raises the logits of certain tokens. One of those tokens is sampled. The token is fed back in as the next input. A different feature fires on it.

The loop closes through the token stream, outside the model. The paper adds that the model never learned these assemblies to work together — they interact because of patterns in the training data.

The simplest case is one node [[self-exciting-feature-loop]]: a base64 feature raises tokens like Qg and zA, which would make it fire again [[fig-55]]. Two nodes without any Unicode involved: A/0/207 on all-caps word pieces and A/0/358 on underscores, producing ARRAY_MAX_VALUE [[fig-56]].

Four nodes give HTML [[html-feature-automaton]]. A/0/20 fires on open tags and predicts tag names. A/0/0 fires on tag names and predicts tag closes. A/0/30 fires on tag closes and predicts whitespace. A/0/494 fires on whitespace and predicts new tag opens. A sample this might produce is `<div>\n\t\t<span>` [[fig-58]].

The paper names its own gap: when A/0/0 emits a token like href, the system moves to a state these four nodes do not describe. This is the main path, not the automaton.

And the tidiness is a choice of zoom [[dictionary-resolution]]. These are A/0 features, from a dictionary of 512 — not overcomplete. The paper says the same system in A/1 would be much more complex.

chapters.title: Grade one evidence for a claim about time
chapters.body:
The paper runs three grades of downstream evidence, and the tokenizer branch gets only the weakest.

Grade one is the logit weight: a linear approximation of a feature's push on each vocabulary token, and the paper itself lists three ways it could overstate a feature's real influence.

Grade two is [[feature-ablation]]. One feature's own contribution — its activation times its dictionary direction — is subtracted from the MLP activation vector, and the rest of the forward pass is run [[eq-feature-ablation]]. The change in per-token loss is measured, not approximated. That operation is well defined only because the decomposition writes an activation as a bias plus a weighted sum of unit-norm directions, so there is a single term belonging to one feature and nothing else [[linear-feature-decomposition]].

Grade three is [[pinned-feature-sampling]]: hold one feature at its maximum observed value and sample.

For the digit feature, grade one is nearly the right instrument. The claim being made is a claim about logit weights — that ten particular tokens sit lower than they otherwise would.

For the automata it is not. The claim is about a sequence unfolding over positions. Logit weights show that feature A raises tokens which would make feature B fire. They do not show that the sequence runs when the model is left to generate.

The tool that would show it is already in the paper. Pinning A/1/3450 high and sampling from the prefix 1,2,3,…,10 produced Arabic script [[fig-43]]. The same operation on A/0/20 would produce a string that could be checked against an HTML parser, and the four-node system makes a checkable prediction about that string.

It is not reported. That the tool exists and was not turned on the automata is my observation, not a shortcoming the paper acknowledges.

What the logit weight evidence does keep is the structural guarantee. Nothing about logits entered the autoencoder's loss [[activations-only-decomposition]], so agreement between where a feature fires and what it writes was never fitted. That protects the reading from being a dataset artifact. It does not turn a described loop into a measured one.

i-an-evaluation-redesigned-then-contradi.title: The two controls, at full resolution
i-an-evaluation-redesigned-then-contradi.intro: The parent gave the shape of both controls and the numbers they returned. This level goes inside them: what the weight shuffle actually destroys and what it leaves intact, which of the three comparison panels can carry evidence at all, how the single-token predicate is computed and on which examples, and what the importance weights arithmetically do to the sample they are applied to.

chapters.title: What the shuffle destroys, and what it leaves standing
chapters.body:
The control is built by [[weight-shuffling]]: take each weight matrix of the trained one-layer model and randomly permute its entries in place.

Note what that is not. It is not resampling weights from a fitted distribution. Permutation preserves the exact multiset of numbers in each matrix — the same marginal histogram, the same scale, the same parameter count — and changes only which position holds which number.

The paper states the reason directly in a footnote: this guarantees the distributions of individual weights match, so any difference traces to structure rather than to scale. A Gaussian-resampled control would not have that guarantee, and a difference could then be blamed on the weights having the wrong magnitude.

So the shuffle isolates arrangement. What it leaves standing is everything outside the weights.

The dataset is unchanged. The tokenizer is unchanged. Activations are still collected from the same corpus at the same layer, and dictionary learning is still run on them with the same objective. That is the whole point: whatever the [[randomized-transformer]] yields must have come from the data, since the model no longer computes anything it learned.

One thing survives that is easy to miss. Token identity survives.

Shuffling the embedding matrix hands each token a vector assembled from the trained pool of entries, but distinct tokens still receive distinct vectors, and the MLP is still a fixed deterministic map. The activation at a position therefore remains a specific, repeatable function of the current token and its context — an arbitrary function, but not a random one.

That is my reading rather than the paper's phrasing, and it matters for what follows. Nothing about "no learned computation" stops dictionary learning from carving out a direction that tracks a particular token. The control removes the model's structure; it does not remove the thing a decomposition can most easily latch onto.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?
Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

chapters.title: Three panels, and which one can carry evidence
chapters.body:
[[fig-70]] compares the real features against the randomized ones on three scores at once: the automated activation score, the automated logit accuracy, and the human rubric.

Take them in order of how much they can say.

The logit panel is [[automated-logit-scoring]]: given only the written explanation, a model guesses which unseen tokens the unit promotes, scored against a half-and-half mix of top positive logit tokens and random ones, so 50% is chance. The randomized model sits at 0.50. The paper calls this unsurprising by the very nature of its random weights.

It is more than unsurprising. The path from an MLP direction to the logits runs through a scrambled down-projection and unembedding, so there is no fact of the matter to predict. The panel cannot separate an interpretable randomized feature from an uninterpretable one. It confirms the shuffle worked, which is a manipulation check rather than evidence.

The rubric panel is [[manual-interpretability-scoring]], and its scale is partly closed to the randomized model. Of the 14 available points, item 3 awards up to 3 for consistency of positive logit effects and item 4 awards 1 for separation between consistent and inconsistent ones. A randomized feature must score zero on both.

So up to 4 of 14 points are unavailable to one side by construction. The paper says this itself, and uses it to explain why the randomized model's non-zero cluster scores below the real features here but not under the automated grader.

That leaves one panel where both populations can score on a level scale. It is the activation score, and it goes to the randomized model — roughly 0.62 median against 0.57.

Where the number sits is worth noting. In the main text, the control is reported as a win on the strength of the authors saying they could not construct sensible interpretations of the non-single-token features, with readers invited to check the visualizations. The main-text activation figure [[fig-40]] carries two legend entries, features and neurons. The randomized median lives in the appendix.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?

chapters.title: A split drawn on the top interval
chapters.body:
The predicate is exact. A unit counts as one of the [[single-token-features]] if, across all 20 examples in its top activation interval, the token carrying the largest activation is the same token every time.

Read where that is computed. It is computed on the top band only — the [[top-dataset-examples]] regime that the whole [[activation-interval]] scheme exists because it flatters.

That is not fatal, and the direction of the error runs the paper's way rather than against it. A unit could be dominated by one token at its maximum and mixed further down, which would put a mixed unit into the single-token bin. The paper claims the opposite holds for the randomized model: its single-token features are more truly single token, firing for the same token even in the weakest intervals. No number is attached to that claim.

The strongest thing in the defence is that the predicate is applied to both populations. The real features are partitioned by the same rule, not left whole while the randomized ones are carved up. On the non-single-token side, the paper reports that the real features score higher and the randomized ones look like the polysemantic neurons.

What is not reported: what fraction of the real features fall in the single-token bin, how the two populations compare inside it beyond a described high-scoring peak, or the medians on either side of the split. The reversal is read off histogram shape.

Then there is what the split is asked to do twice. The paper also reads the abundance of single-token features in the randomized model as fitting the hypothesis that dictionary learning learns the features of the dataset rather than the representations of the transformer.

Those two uses are consistent. The randomized model has only data structure, so of course that is what it recovers.

But it leaves the defence resting on the deflationary reading being true of the control, with the case for the real model being that its features are not like that. My reading is that the split is credible as a mechanism and weak as a test, because the mechanism was named after the result it explains.

sections.title: How Interpretable is the Typical Feature?

chapters.title: The correct weighting, and what it removes
chapters.body:
[[importance-scoring]] is specified precisely enough to work through.

Every token from a random example gets weight 1. Every token from a feature-interval example gets weight equal to the unit's density times the probability of that interval. Density is the fraction of tokens over a large sample on which the unit fires. Interval probability turns the unit's distribution of non-zero activations into a categorical distribution over the intervals and reads off the mass in that band. Top-activating tokens shown out of context inherit the weight of the top interval. Those weights then go into the same [[spearman-correlation]] used everywhere else — a correlation on ranks, so it asks whether the predicted ordering of activations matches the true ordering, not whether the numbers agree.

What the weights reconstruct is the score the sample would have produced had it been drawn from text at random.

It was not drawn that way. Of the 60 prediction examples, 6 come from the top interval, 2 from each of the other 12, 10 are completely random, and 20 are top-activating tokens out of context.

Walk one case, as an illustration of mine rather than a figure from the paper. Take a feature with density $10^{-4}$, and suppose a hundredth of its non-zero activations fall in a given interval. Each token from that interval carries weight $10^{-6}$. Fifty examples carry weights of roughly that order; ten carry weight 1. At nine tokens each, that is 90 tokens summing to 90, against 450 tokens summing to about $4.5\times10^{-4}$.

The random tokens hold essentially all of the mass. Drop the density to $10^{-6}$, the low end of the paper's stated range, and the designed examples fall another hundredfold behind.

So the correction is correct, and it deletes almost the entire sample the evaluation was built to collect. What is left being scored is ninety tokens of ordinary text, on which the feature almost certainly never fires.

The isolation the automated score depends on, [[no-activation-leakage]], is untouched by any of this. The problem is not leakage. It is that the honest weighting leaves nearly nothing to grade.

chapters.title: What the density explanation settles, and what it does not
chapters.body:
The mechanism behind [[importance-scoring-degeneracy]] follows from the rank correlation.

On random examples, 88% of a feature's true activations are zero, against 54% for neurons; the medians are about 91% and 58%. When 88% of the true values are tied at zero, the ranking is dominated by that one tie block. An explanation predicting zero everywhere agrees with it. Where the prediction is constant, no correlation is defined at all, and the paper assigns zero in those cases — so the degeneracy pushes in both directions at once.

The paper adds the other half plainly: because the true rate of firing is so low, an explanation is heavily penalised for even a small false positive rate. The corrected score rewards saying what a unit does not fire for.

A second mechanism operates that the paper does not name, and this is my reading. The interval weight is proportional to the unit's own [[feature-density]]. A dense neuron keeps its interval examples at weights near its density times the interval probability, not at $10^{-6}$. The reweighting therefore hollows out the feature sample far more than the neuron sample, so after correction the two are not being graded on comparable evidence. It points the same way as the paper's explanation.

What the density argument settles: the collapse is predicted by rarity alone, with no claim about explanation quality entering. A perfectly explained rare feature would show it too.

What it does not settle is which number to report. The unweighted score oversamples the firing regime by orders of magnitude. The weighted score in [[fig-71]] is dominated by the regime where nothing happens. Neither estimates the quantity a reader wants, and the paper does not offer a third.

One thing does hold up. Unlike the randomized control, this comparison does not reverse: 0.28 against 0.04 is still a wide gap in the features' favour, on the measure the authors argue is degenerate.

What the pair of controls costs is the automated grader's standing as an independent check. Both times, reading it required an argument supplied after the result. The measure the paper leans on hardest — the blinded rubric, weighed against [[automated-interpretability]] precisely because it is more trusted and less scalable — is untouched by either control, and rests on one annotator who is one of the authors.
